fullPassage: Caves hold archives of climate history. Since they maintain a stable environment, they can preserve these records for long periods. Most of the records are found in stalagmites, cone-shaped formations on the floor of caves. These structures are formed when rainwater full of minerals from the soil drips into caves and crystallizes. As they grow, they trap the chemical signatures of the rainwater in their layers, which provide information about the climatic conditions at the time the water was deposited. By analyzing the composition of each layer, scientists have gained insights about temperature and precipitation patterns in different periods. For example, they found evidence of an unusually cold period during the 16th century in a stalagmite in southern Germany, whose oxygen composition suggested less evaporation due to lower temperatures. Such analyses enable climate researchers to compare past climate trends with current ones. They are crucial, as they can be used to develop more accurate climate models and improve predictions about how the climate might change in the future.
